summary_html: Agency **files a court petition** to open a **dependency** (or similar) case. Federal funding frameworks (IV-E/ASFA) link court oversight, reasonable-efforts findings, and permanency timelines to downstream actions.
authority_html:
- **ASFA / SSA Title IV-E** — court findings; timelines; permanency planning  
- **CFSR (45 CFR Part 1355)** — federal review of court/agency performance measures

primary_citations.citation_text: Hawaii — HRS Chapter 587A, Child Protective Act
Haw. Rev. Stat. § 587A-26, Temporary foster custody hearing

provisions_triggered.name: Due Process / Law of the Land

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.court: Intermediate Court of Appeals of Hawai'i
key_cases.holding: The ICA affirmed an order of family supervision, holding that a chapter 587 petition is verified by a declaration under penalty of perjury, that threatened harm alone suffices to sustain the petition, and that DHS's disclosure of case information to the police was not a ground for dismissal absent particularized objection.
key_cases.relevance: It sets the verification and pleading requirements for the petition that opens a Hawai'i dependency case.
key_cases.quote: Thus, allegations of actual harm are not required to sustain a petition for family supervision and allegations of threatened harm would suffice.

key_cases.holding: The court held that under article I, section 5 of the Hawai'i Constitution indigent parents have a right to court-appointed counsel in termination proceedings, and that the family court abused its discretion by not appointing counsel until nineteen months after DHS petitioned for temporary foster custody.
key_cases.relevance: Filing the petition is the point at which the indigent parent's right to appointed counsel attaches, so the petition decision has immediate due-process consequences.
key_cases.quote: indigent parents are guaranteed the right to court-appointed counsel in termination proceedings

key_cases.holding: The court held that counsel must be appointed for an indigent parent when DHS files a petition for family supervision, not merely when it seeks foster custody, and that failure to do so is structural error requiring vacatur of the foster-custody and termination orders.
key_cases.relevance: The filing of any petition that can lead to custody or termination, including a family supervision petition, triggers the appointment duty.
key_cases.quote: The family court's failure to appoint Mother counsel when DHS filed its petition for family supervision was structural error and cannot be deemed harmless.

key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed denial of absolute and qualified immunity to social workers who failed to give a mother notice of the detention hearing and then told the juvenile court her whereabouts were unknown, holding that giving notice is a mandatory, non-discretionary act and that the right against judicial deception was clearly established.
key_cases.relevance: Filing a petition and obtaining detention orders requires truthful representations and actual notice to the parent.
key_cases.quote: An individual has a well-established constitutional right to be free from deception in the presentation of evidence during juvenile dependency proceedings.

key_cases.case_name: In the Interest of the P Children
key_cases.holding: The court held that an indigent parent's constitutional right to counsel is not invoked for structural-error purposes until the parent appears and engages in the case, including complying with the court's indigency process, affirmed the permanent custody and adoption orders because the years-long proceeding was fundamentally fair, and directed family courts to make an indigency determination at a parent's first appearance.
key_cases.relevance: It supplies the operational rule that follows the filing of a chapter 587A petition: the family court must determine indigency at the parent's first appearance, and must appoint counsel whenever indigency is uncertain or the parent resists the inquiry.
key_cases.quote: we direct family courts to make an indigency determination at a parent's first appearance in a chapter 587A proceeding that substantially affects parental rights

key_cases.holding: The court held that, as an aspect of procedural due process, a parent who needs an interpreter must be provided one at any family court proceeding where parental rights are substantially affected, a question resolved case by case rather than by a bright-line test, but affirmed the award of foster custody to DHS because the mother showed neither a need for an interpreter nor substantial prejudice and DHS proved harm by a preponderance of the evidence.
key_cases.relevance: This is the pre-T.M. authority holding that due process protections attach whenever a family court proceeding substantially affects parental rights, decided case by case with no bright-line test; In re T.M. (2014) later replaced that case-by-case approach for the appointment of counsel.
key_cases.quote: Procedural due process requires that an individual whose rights are at stake understand the nature of the proceedings he or she faces.
